title: Efficient Sphere-Effect Based Information Diffusion Prediction on Large-scale Social Networks

problem.claim: Information diffusion prediction aims to forecast user participation in information sharing on social networks.

gap.claim: Existing methods may rely on sequential diffusion modeling, simplify differentiated participant influences, and use whole-graph user relationships that include unnecessary information and are inefficient for large-scale networks.

contributions.claim: SILN is a scalable sphere-based model for information diffusion prediction on large social networks.
SILN integrates structural and temporal sphere effects to learn an enhanced cascade representation.
SILN uses cascade-specific subgraphs for efficient learning and an optimized graph storage technique for constant-time neighbor access and about 30% lower storage cost in practice.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors describe SILN as a novel and scalable model.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Extensive experiments on six real-world datasets reportedly validate SILN's performance.
The authors report that SILN consistently outperforms seven state-of-the-art competitors in prediction performance.
The authors report exceptional time and space efficiency on million-node social networks.

narrative_sequence.summary: Information diffusion prediction supports forecasting participation in social-network information sharing.
Existing approaches model user relationships, historical interactions, and diffusion-process context.
These approaches can oversimplify participant influences and incur inefficient whole-graph computation.
SILN addresses the limitations with structural and temporal sphere effects, cascade-specific subgraphs, and optimized graph storage.
Experiments on six real-world datasets report improved prediction performance and time and space efficiency relative to seven competitors, including on million-node networks.

source_observation.claim: The method reduces whole-graph computation to cascade-specific subgraphs.

interpretation.claim: Task-specific locality can reduce computational overhead when full-graph information is largely irrelevant.

application.claim: For large-scale graph prediction, consider extracting subgraphs tailored to each prediction instance.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish when cascade-specific subgraphs may omit information needed for accurate prediction.

source_observation.claim: The storage technique enables constant-time neighbor access and reduces storage cost by about 30% in practice.

interpretation.claim: Data-structure optimization can complement model changes in improving large-graph efficiency.

application.claim: When deploying graph models at scale, optimize graph access and storage alongside learning algorithms.

exception.claim: The reported storage reduction is described only as practical and is not characterized across datasets or workloads.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the six datasets, evaluation metrics, or experimental settings.
The abstract does not describe the seven competitors or quantify prediction improvements.
The abstract does not provide details about the sphere effects, subgraph extraction procedure, or storage implementation.
